desc:
A school has n students labelled 0 to n - 1. Each entry friendships[i] = [a, b] says that students a and b are friends (friendship works both ways).

A friend circle is a group of students in which any two can be linked by a chain of friends, and that cannot be enlarged: nobody outside the group is a friend of someone inside it. A student with no friends forms a circle of one.

Return the number of students in the largest friend circle.

n = 5, friendships = [[0,1],[1,2],[3,4]]

result = 3     (circles: {0,1,2} and {3,4})
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b < n and a ≠ b
No pair of students appears twice
hints: Every student belongs to exactly one circle, and two students share a circle exactly when a chain of friendships links them.
Give every student its own group at the start. For each friendship, merge the group of a with the group of b. This is the idea behind union-find.
Keep a size next to each group root and add the two sizes when you merge. Track the largest size seen, starting at 1 because a lone student is a circle of one.
editorial: Use a disjoint-set (union-find) structure with parent[i] = i and size[i] = 1. For every friendship find the two roots; if they differ, attach the smaller tree under the larger one and add the sizes. After each successful merge the new size is a candidate for the answer. The answer starts at 1, which covers the case without any friendship.

With path compression and union by size, each operation is almost constant time, so the whole thing is O(n + m · α(n)). A BFS or DFS over an adjacency list gives the same answer, but union-find needs no adjacency list and generalises to harder problems where edges arrive one by one.
